books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: John L. O'Sullivan, “Annexation,” United States Magazine and Democratic Review, July 1845

stimulus.source_note: John L. O'Sullivan, “Annexation,” United States Magazine and Democratic Review, July 1845. Public domain.
stimulus.text: Texas is now ours. Already, before these words are written, her Convention has undoubtedly ratified the acceptance, by her of our proffered invitation into the Union... And that claim is by the right of our manifest destiny to overspread the continent allotted by Providence for the free development of our yearly multiplying millions. California will, probably, next fall away from the loose adhesion which, in such a country as Mexico, holds a remote province in a slight equivocal kind of dependence on the metropolis.

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim excerpt from John L. O'Sullivan, “Annexation,” July 1845, public domain
stem: The author's argument in the passage rests most directly on which claim about the United States?

options.text: The United States had signed a treaty with Mexico that allowed it to take California.
options.misconception: Mexico had agreed to nothing of the sort; O'Sullivan only predicts that California will fall away.

options.text: Providence had allotted the whole continent to the American people.
Both political parties agreed that Texas should join the Union at once.
options.misconception: Annexation was fiercely debated; O'Sullivan writes against the opposition to it.

options.text: Texas had voted to remain an independent republic.
options.misconception: The passage says Texas accepted the invitation into the Union.

rationales.A: O'Sullivan only predicts California will fall away from Mexico; no treaty with Mexico is mentioned anywhere in the passage.
rationales.B: O'Sullivan says the claim rests on “our manifest destiny to overspread the continent allotted by Providence,” so the argument is that God assigned the continent to Americans. Background: this 1845 editorial gave the expansionist idea its famous name.
rationales.C: The passage never claims the parties agreed. Background: annexation was fiercely debated in Congress in 1845; O'Sullivan argues from Providence, not from consensus.
rationales.D: The passage opens by saying Texas accepted “our proffered invitation into the Union,” so Texas chose statehood, not independence.
rationales.general:
1. Find the reason O'Sullivan gives. He says the claim rests on “our manifest destiny to overspread the continent allotted by Providence.”
2. Read that phrase plainly. Providence means God, and the continent was allotted, or assigned, to Americans.
3. Test the other choices against the words. No treaty is named, nothing in the passage says the parties agreed, and Texas joined the Union.
Remember: when a writer says “by the right of,” the next words name the right — here, a God-given claim to the whole continent.
